lessons.words: bond – strong connection; swallow – tolerate; grudged – gave unwillingly; obvious – clear; allowance – an amount of money given regularly; sympathize – feel sorry for somebody; mum – quiet, silent; nominate – propose, suggest someone’s name; abide by – accept; conscience – something that tells you whether you are right or wrong; defence – something said in support; claim – deemed as right; seldom – rarely; revenge – something made to make somebody suffer; annoyed – slightly angry; wretched – extremely annoying; beast – an animal; ruin – something that causes loss; proposed – suggested; realized – became aware of; dignity – respectful manner; disability – physical weakness; begotten – got, earned; distressing gain – dishonestly obtained profit; exploited – unearthed; charm – attract, influence; shackled – chained; fished out – drew or pulled out from; sack – a large bag; lair – resting place; dash – (short) race
lessons.notes: Unit 5 has a prose story 'Justice Above Self' by Munshi Premchand (pp. 1–15). Jumman and Algu are close friends. Jumman's aunt gives him her property on the condition that he looks after her, but he and his wife neglect her. She takes the case to the Panchayat, where Algu is chosen as the Panch. Later Algu's bullock dies after Sahu buys it, and Jumman, now the head Panch, gives a fair judgement even though Algu is his enemy. The lesson teaches justice, fairness and honesty. The poem 'Justice' by Praveen Kumar (pp. 12–15) says that justice is a right and must not be bought or sold for money or favour. Figures of speech (simile and personification) and the complex sentence are taught in this unit.
ab: Before you read – Enact the following scene (p. 1)
Enact the following scene: King Rama’s court. Rama, Laxman and courtiers are sitting. A servant comes and speaks about the washerman who insulted Sita. Take the roles and act it out.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. (ನಾಟಕೀಯ ಅಭಿನಯ ಚಟುವಟಿಕೆ.)
Check your comprehension – Paragraphs 1 to 3 (p. 3)
1. How was the bond of friendship between Jumman and Algu?
Their bond of friendship was so strong that when either of them went away from the village, the other looked after his family. Both were greatly respected in the village.
2. On what condition did Jumman’s aunt transfer her property to him?
She transferred her property to him on the understanding that she would stay with him and he would look after her.
3. What did the aunt demand to set up a separate kitchen?
She demanded a monthly allowance.
4. What made the old lady angry?
Jumman was indifferent to her, his wife grudged even the little food she needed, and Jumman shamelessly said that his wife knew best how to run the house. These insults made the old lady angry.
5. How did people react to the old lady when she went about explaining her plight?
Some sympathized with her, some laughed at her, and a few advised her to make up with her nephew and his wife.
6. Why did Algu Chowdhary say that he could not go against Jumman?
Algu said that he could not go against Jumman because Jumman was his best friend.
Check your comprehension – Paragraphs 5 to 6 (p. 4)
1. What was Jumman’s opinion about the Panch?
Jumman believed that the voice of the Panch is the voice of God, and he said he would abide by the decision of the Panch.
2. Was the old lady right in nominating Algu as the Panch knowing very well that he was Jumman’s best friend? If ‘yes’, why? If ‘no’, why?
Yes. The old lady was right because she knew that a Panch knows neither enemy nor friend, and that Algu would not kill his conscience for the sake of friendship. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
3. What decision did Algu give after listening to Jumman and his aunt?
Algu decided that Jumman must pay his aunt a monthly allowance, or else the property would go back to her.
4. Why were Algu and Jumman seldom seen together after the Panchayat?
The bond of friendship between them was broken. Jumman saw Algu as an enemy and wanted to take revenge.
Check your comprehension – Paragraphs 7 to 10 (p. 5)
1. Who did Algu sell his bullock to?
Algu sold his bullock to Sanju Sahu, a cart driver of the village.
2. What happened to the bullock bought by Sahu from Algu?
The bullock died within a month of being bought by Sahu.
3. Who did Sahu nominate as the head Panch?
Sahu nominated Jumman as the head Panch.
4. How did Algu feel hearing the judgement?
Algu was very happy. He could not contain his feelings and loudly said, ‘Victory to the Panchayat. This is justice. God lives in the voice of the Panch.’
C1. Think about the text (p. 6)
1. ‘I am not wanted in your house’ – a. Who is referred to as ‘I’?
The old lady, Jumman’s aunt.
1. ‘I am not wanted in your house’ – b. Where was the speaker?
The speaker was in Jumman’s house.
1. ‘I am not wanted in your house’ – c. What did the speaker demand?
She demanded a monthly allowance so that she could set up a separate kitchen.
2. ‘How can I go against him?’ – a. Who said it?
Algu Chowdhary said it.
2. ‘How can I go against him?’ – b. Who does ‘him’ refer to?
‘Him’ refers to Jumman.
2. ‘How can I go against him?’ – c. Why was he not ready to go against the person?
Because Jumman was his best friend.
C1. Think about the text (p. 7)
3. ‘I had become your enemy’ – a. Who had become the enemy of whom?
Jumman had become the enemy of Algu.
3. ‘I had become your enemy’ – b. When did the enmity start?
It started after the last Panchayat, when Algu’s judgement went against Jumman.
3. ‘I had become your enemy’ – c. What caused the enmity between them?
Algu’s judgement in the Panchayat that Jumman must pay the monthly allowance to his aunt.
4. ‘I will abide by her decision’ – a. Who agreed to abide by her decision?
Jumman agreed to abide by her decision.
4. ‘I will abide by her decision’ – b. Where did the person make the statement?
He made the statement at the Panchayat held under the old banyan tree.
4. ‘I will abide by her decision’ – c. What decision is referred to here?
The decision of his aunt in choosing the head Panch (she nominated Algu Chowdhary).
5. ‘He brought us nothing but ruin’ – a. Who said this?
Sanju Sahu said this.
5. ‘He brought us nothing but ruin’ – b. Who was this said to?
It was said to Algu Chowdhary.
5. ‘He brought us nothing but ruin’ – c. How did ‘he’ bring ruin to his owner?
The bullock died within a month after Sahu bought it, so Sahu suffered a loss.
C2. Think over the following questions and try to form your own answers (p. 7)
1. What would you have done in case you were the Panch in place of Algu Chowdhary?
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: I would have judged fairly, based on the facts and truth, and would not allow friendship or enmity to influence my decision.
2. What values do you learn from the lesson? Write them down.
Justice, honesty, fairness, impartiality, courage to speak the truth, forgiveness and reconciliation, respect and care for elders, and the value of friendship.
3. Do you like the way Jumman’s wife treated the old lady? If ‘yes’, give reasons. If ‘no’, give reasons.
No. The old lady was not treated with love or respect. Her food was grudged and she was neglected, even though Jumman had promised to look after her. ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
4. Assume yourself to be Jumman. Narrate how you would have looked after the old lady.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: I would have respected her, given her food and medicines on time, provided her a separate room and spoken kindly with her, and I would keep my promise to care for her.
5. Discuss in groups how old people should be cared for. Write down the outcome of your discussion in four or five sentences.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: Old people should be treated with love and respect. They need proper food, medicine and a comfortable place to live. Family members should spend time with them and listen to them. Their opinions should be respected and they should not be left alone or neglected.
Vocabulary – Homophones: Fill in the blanks using the correct word given in brackets (p. 8)
A hunter went to a forest in search of a game. ……… (There / Their), he saw a …… (deer / dear) behind a big tree.
There; deer
He …… (new / knew) he could no more continue and needed …… (some / sum) rest.
knew; some
He …… (wrested / rested) under a shady tree and soon fell asleep.

It was …… (night / knight) when he woke up.
night
He …… (excepted / accepted) his failure in catching the animal and returned home empty handed.
accepted
Speak well – Offering advice: S1. Practise the dialogue taking roles (p. 8)
S1. Imagine you are a doctor and your friend Ravi is a patient. Read the dialogue and practise it taking roles.

Practice activity in pairs (Doctor and Ravi). Model: Doctor – ‘You should always consult a doctor before you start taking medicines. Don’t ever go for self medication.’ Ravi – ‘Sorry doctor. Henceforth I shall consult a doctor for my health-related problems.’
Speak well – Offering advice: S2 (p. 9)

S2. A friend of yours has failed in the examination. He/She is feeling desperate. Speak to him/her to know the problem and try to pacify him/her. Use the clues: father ill, studies hampered, not his/her mistake, failure is not the end of everything, try again, will come out with flying colours, ready to give help.

Model: ‘I know your father has been ill and your studies were hampered. It is not your mistake. Failure is not the end of everything. Try again and you will come out with flying colours. I am always ready to help you.’
Language in use – Complex sentences: Task 1 (p. 9–10)
Task 1. Identify the main clause and the subordinate clause in each of the sentences taken from the lesson given above (page 98). [Text correction: ‘page 98’ should read ‘pages 1–5’.]

1. Main: ‘His wife grudged even the little food’ | Subordinate: ‘that the old lady needed for survival’ (relative clause)
2. Main: ‘But I also know’ | Subordinate: ‘that you will not kill your conscience for the sake of friendship’ (noun clause)
3. Main: ‘Jumman had an old aunt’ | Subordinate: ‘who had some property’ (relative clause)
4. Main: ‘My son, it is now obvious’ | Subordinate: ‘that I am not wanted in your house’ (noun clause)
5. Main: ‘Now my aunt is claiming a monthly allowance from me’ | Subordinate: ‘which I can’t pay’ (relative clause)
Task 2. Read the story carefully and pick out the complex sentences you come across. Classify the main clauses and subordinate clauses in the sentences you have picked out.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: (1) ‘So strong was their bond of friendship that when either of them went away from the village, the other looked after his family.’ Main: ‘So strong was their bond of friendship’; Subordinate: ‘that when either of them went away from the village, the other looked after his family’. (2) ‘The old lady went about meeting people explaining her case.’ Main: ‘The old lady went about meeting people’; Subordinate: ‘explaining her case’ (participle phrase). (3) ‘Algu decided that Jumman must pay his aunt a monthly allowance.’ Main: ‘Algu decided’; Subordinate: ‘that Jumman must pay his aunt a monthly allowance’.
Read and respond (p. 10–11)
Task 1. Collect and read similar newspaper excerpts that speak of injustice meted out to innocents or that tell you about justice done to the people who are just, righteous and honest.
Activity: students collect newspaper cuttings or news items on injustice or justice and read them in class. Marks as per the teacher’s evaluation.
Practise writing (p. 11)
Write a paragraph noting the good qualities of your best friend. Use the clues: gentle, soft spoken, always helpful, honest, God fearing, clean, disciplined.

Model: My best friend, Algu, is a gentle and soft spoken boy. He is always helpful to others and is very honest. He is God fearing and keeps himself clean. He is also disciplined in his studies and daily routine. I am proud to have him as my friend.
Task 2. Writing dialogues: Write the story in the form of a play, beginning as given (Jumman – My dear friend Algu, I am going to visit my relatives…).

Model: Jumman – My dear friend Algu, I am going to visit my relatives in the neighbouring village. It may not be possible for me to return home for two days. I request you to look after my family and cattle for two days. Algu – Don’t worry Jumman. It is my pleasure being of some service to a good friend like you. Jumman – Thank you, Algu. My aunt is staying with us, please take care of her also. Algu – Yes, I will.
Poetry – Before you read (p. 12)
Make a list of things and obligations that cannot be bought with money.
Blood, love, friendship, kindness, trust, honesty, respect, a parent’s affection, a teacher’s blessings, good health and justice (values and obligations that money cannot buy).
Understand the poem (p. 14)
1. When is justice reduced to trade?
Justice is reduced to trade when it is obtained in exchange for something, such as money or a favour. Then it is no longer justice.
2. What is the poet’s concern about justice expressed in the line ‘A distressing gain through loss’?
The poet is worried that justice is gained through dishonest means, as profit that causes loss to others. Such justice is not real justice.
3. What kind of a right is justice?
Justice is an inherent right, a natural right that belongs to every human being.
4. What kind of justice is dead, according to the poet?
Justice with no heart for truth and no dash for the right cause is dead.
5. How does the poet describe justice?
The poet describes justice as cool like ice and still like rock; as gold strains bound in mud; and as a thing that never reaches its goal by itself.
6. What present status of justice worries the poet?
Justice is shackled to greed and bribe, it is fished out from popular mood and it is lost in the jungle of lightless night. It is exploited and sold for profit.
Read and appreciate (p. 14)
1. The poet compares justice to ‘gold strains’, ‘ice’ and ‘rock’. Why?
Justice is precious like gold, but it is covered with dirt (mud) from greed and dishonesty. Ice and rock show that justice is cool, firm and unmoved by bribe, greed or hardship.
2. The poet says, ‘No easy road to charm her soul While hardship makes her no more justice.’ Do you find his opinion about justice contrasting? If so, why? If not, why? Discuss in groups.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: Yes. Justice is firm like rock and cannot be charmed easily, yet hardship and greed make it lose its meaning. This contrast shows that justice can be weakened when it is not protected.
Figures of speech – examples given in the lesson (p. 14–15; explanation in the book, no separate exercise)
Example: ‘Like gold strains bound in mud’, ‘She is cool like ice’, ‘And still like rock’.
Simile. The poet compares justice directly with gold strains, ice and rock using ‘like’.
Example: ‘Like rat, caught in the sack of death’, ‘Like deer, caught in lion’s lair’.
Simile. Justice is compared directly with a rat and a deer using ‘like’.
Example: ‘She (justice) never reaches Self by herself.’
Personification. An abstract notion (justice) is given the qualities of a living being that can reach or not reach its goal.

lessons.t: Unit 6 · The Noble Bishop (Prose) & Nobleness Enkindleth Nobleness (Poem)
lessons.au: Victor Hugo (Prose, play); James Russell Lowell (Poem)
lessons.words: Jean Valjean – (pronounced ‘Zhon Valzhon’); convict – a person imprisoned for a crime; galley – ship usually rowed by prisoners; alcove – a partly enclosed space in a room; stifling – suffocating; mantel – a shelf above a fireplace; devour – eat up something greedily; sentence (v) – punishment given by a court of law; sob – draw in breath noisily while crying; lash – strike with a whip; hound – a type of dog used in hunting; reflect – think deeply; shudder – shiver with cold, fear, etc.; conscience – a person’s awareness of right and wrong; contemplate – consider something thoughtfully; sergeant – police officer; strive – try very hard; oppressed – treated in an unfair way; downtrodden – ruled or controlled tyrannically; destitute – a person without money, food and shelter; behold – to see something; outcast – a person expelled from the community; dread – fear of something bad that might happen; hath – has; shalt – shall; thou – you; partake – share; nay – no or not; ere – before; prying – searching; enkindleth – kindles; hast – has; slew – killed someone violently; thee – you; yearn – long for; thou art – you are; avenge – take revenge; decree – judgement
lessons.notes: Unit 6 has a play 'The Noble Bishop' by Victor Hugo (pp. 16–22). A convict, Jean Valjean, is given food and shelter by a kind Bishop, but he steals the silverware and runs away. The police bring him back, and the Bishop says the silver was a gift and gives him the candlesticks too. Jean Valjean promises to become an honest man. The poem 'Nobleness Enkindleth Nobleness' by James Russell Lowell (pp. 27–31) tells how Yussouf, a noble man, gives shelter and gold to a stranger who has killed his son, and the stranger is moved to repent. The lesson teaches kindness, generosity and forgiveness.
ab: Before you read – Pet animal (p. 16)
Which is the animal that is referred to in the above incident? a. a cat b. a dog c. a horse d. a rabbit
c. a horse (Soundarya is a pony).
Why do you think the pet has entered only your compound and not that of others?
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: Because the pony trusted me. I was kind to her and the other residents, so she came to my compound for help.
How would you treat the wounded pet? Discuss with your teacher and classmates.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: I would clean the wound, give her water, keep her in a safe and quiet place and call a vet or inform the owner at once.
Check your comprehension – C1. Work in pairs (p. 21)
1. Who was Jean Valjean?
Jean Valjean was a convict. He had been in the galleys for nineteen years for stealing bread to feed his starving sister’s children.
2. Who brought the silver candlesticks from the mantel?
Baptistine, the Bishop’s sister, brought the silver candlesticks from the mantel.
3. What did the stranger steal from the Bishop’s place?
He stole the silverware (the silver plates) from the table.
4. Why was Jean Valjean surprised at the Bishop’s behaviour the next morning?
The police brought him back, but the Bishop did not accuse him. He called him ‘friend’, said that the silver was a gift and even gave him the silver candlesticks.
5. Why was Jean Valjean finally set free?
The Bishop told the sergeant that the silverware had been given to Jean Valjean by him, so the police set him free.
6. What did Jean Valjean promise the Bishop?
He promised that he would use the silver to become an honest man.
Think about the text – C2 (p. 21)
1. What do you think were Jean Valjean’s feelings when he was called ‘friend’?
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: He was surprised and deeply moved. He felt he was a man again and not a wild beast, and he wept.
2. Why did Jean Valjean say that he was a beast?
Because society treated him like a wild animal in prison. He was chained, lashed like a hound and fed on filth, and he lost his name and his soul.
3. What kind of a person was the Bishop?
The Bishop was kind, compassionate, forgiving, generous and honest. He treated a convict as a brother.
4. Why did Jean Valjean hesitate to steal the silverware at first?
The peaceful, radiant face of the sleeping Bishop troubled his conscience, so he hesitated and was terrified before he stole the silverware.
5. Was there any change in Jean Valjean’s attitude when he left the Bishop? What was the change?
Yes. He became an honest man. He sold the silverware, kept the candlesticks in memory of the Bishop, and worked for the oppressed and the destitute.
Think about the text – C3 (p. 21)
1. Describe the sufferings of Jean Valjean.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: Jean Valjean was sentenced to nineteen years in the galleys for stealing bread to feed his starving sister’s children. He was chained like a wild animal, lashed and fed on filth. He lost his name and his soul. After his release, no one would give him work, and he was starving.
2. Explain how the Bishop reacted when Jean Valjean was brought before him by the police.
The Bishop was glad to see him and called him ‘my friend’. He told the police that the silver was a gift, gave him the candlesticks and asked him to become an honest man.
C4. Say whether the following statements are true or false (p. 22)
1. Jean Valjean was in the galleys only for a few years.
False. He was in the galleys for nineteen years.
2. All the people were kind to Jean Valjean.
False. He was told ‘Get out!’ at every inn, and no one was willing to give him work.
3. The Bishop woke up in the middle of the night.
False. It was Jean Valjean who woke up in the middle of the night.
4. Baptistine said that the silver was stolen.
True.
5. The silverware belonged to Jean Valjean.
False. The silverware belonged to the Bishop, and the Bishop said it belonged to the poor.

Learn grammar through communication – G1. Modals: Say what function each modal serves (p. 24)
1. You may be tired.
Expressing possibility.
2. We can let him go.
Granting permission.
3. You can take these candlesticks.
Granting permission.
4. You may go in peace.
Granting permission.
Learn grammar through communication – G1. Modals: Task 1. Underline the modals used in the dialogue (p. 24–25)
Read the following dialogue and underline the modals used.

may (Yes, you may); may (May I come in, Sir?); must (You must take medicines); can (Can I attend office?); shouldn’t (You shouldn’t); must (You must take rest); should (You should be on liquid diet); should (Should I see you again?); needn’t (You needn’t).
Learn grammar through communication – G2. Types of sentences (p. 25)
1. I am a convict.
Simple sentence (one main clause).
2. I’m a beast now, and they made me what I am.
Compound sentence (two main clauses joined by ‘and’).
3. While we have supper, your bed will be made ready.
Complex sentence (‘while we have supper’ is the subordinate clause; ‘your bed will be made ready’ is the main clause).
Learn grammar through communication – G2. Types of sentences: Task 1 (p. 26)
1. The rain stopped, so we decided to continue our journey.
Compound sentence (two main clauses joined by ‘so’).
2. When I reached home, I was surprised to see Gopi waiting for me.
Complex sentence.
3. Ravi raised his voice and shouted at his friend.
Simple sentence (one subject with two verbs; only one main clause).
4. The teacher advised Uma to study well.
Simple sentence.
5. As Sumathi is blind, the dog is leading her.
Complex sentence.
Learn grammar through communication – G2. Types of sentences: Task 2. Combine the sentences using the conjunctions given in brackets (p. 26)
He opened his box. He took out his new shirt. (and)
He opened his box and took out his new shirt.
Mohan was sick. He stayed at home. (as)
As Mohan was sick, he stayed at home.
Leela worked hard. She could not do well in the exam. (but)
Leela worked hard but she could not do well in the exam.
Sachin scored a century. The spectators applauded him. (when)
When Sachin scored a century, the spectators applauded him.
Let us have supper. By then your bed will be made ready. (while)
Let us have supper while your bed is being made ready.
Learn grammar through communication – G2. Types of sentences: Task 3. Pick out simple, compound and complex sentences from the passage ‘Sweet Smile’ (p. 26)
Pick out the simple, compound and complex sentences from the passage.

Complex: ‘A child smiles not only because it is happy but also because it wants to communicate with loving elders.’; ‘When a child is hungry, it cries.’
Simple: ‘A cheerful smile brings instant attention.’; ‘Any grown-up is instantly motivated to respond to a smiling child.’; ‘It hears a few soothing words and stops crying.’; ‘There is nothing as infectious as a warm smile, even among adults.’; ‘Do you like to smile?’
Compound: ‘Sometimes even serious faces break into a smile and even the smile of a stranger carries the universal message “I care”.’
Poetry – Before you read: Meaning of the words (p. 27)
Find the meaning of these words from a dictionary: pity, forgive, condole, console, grant, amnesty, compassion, mercy, lament, pardon, reprieve, solace, asylum.

pity – feel sorry for someone; forgive – pardon; condole – express sympathy in grief; console – comfort; grant – give; amnesty – an official pardon; compassion – sympathy for the suffering of others; mercy – kindness shown to someone; lament – express sorrow; pardon – forgive; reprieve – cancellation or postponement of punishment; solace – comfort; asylum – shelter and protection.
Understand the poem (p. 29–30)
1. Who came to Yussouf’s tent one night?
A stranger, an outcast in dread, who was hunted by the power of the enemy, came to Yussouf’s tent.
2. What did he say?
He said that he had nowhere to lay his head and asked Yussouf for shelter and food.
3. Did he go to the tent for food and shelter?
Yes, he went to the tent for food and shelter.
4. Was Yussouf called ‘The Good’?
Yes, Yussouf was called ‘The Good’ through all the tribes.
5. Was Yussouf kind to the stranger?
Yes. He entertained him, gave him food and shelter, a swift horse and gold.
6. Did Yussouf believe in God?
Yes. He believed that everything, including the tent, belongs to God.
7. What did Yussouf say, waking up the stranger?
‘Here is gold, my swiftest horse is saddled for thy flight. Depart before the prying day grow bold.’
8. What made the stranger’s face grand?
The inward light that shines from self-conquest, that is, the nobleness of Yussouf’s kindness.
9. Who killed Yussouf’s son?
Ibrahim, the stranger, killed Yussouf’s son.
10. Did Yussouf get angry?
No. Instead of getting angry, he gave the stranger thrice the gold.
11. What did Yussouf say to Ibrahim?
‘Take thrice the gold … Thou art avenged, my first-born, sleep in peace!’
12. Who did Yussouf yearn for day and night?
He yearned for his first-born son.
Read and appreciate (p. 30)
1. How has the poet described the stranger?

The poet describes the stranger as an outcast in dread, whose life was targeted by power; he was homeless, tired and crying. After Yussouf’s kindness, his face became grand with inner light and he kneeled and sobbed.
2. Pick out the lines which show Yussouf’s respect for God.
‘The tent is mine,’ said Yussouf, ‘but no more Than it is God’s’; ‘As I of His who buildeth over these Our tents His glorious roof of night and day’; ‘Balanced and just are all of God’s decrees’.
3. Explain: ‘As one lamp lights another, nor grows less, So nobleness enkindleth nobleness.’
Just as one lamp lights another without becoming less, a noble act inspires another noble act. Goodness spreads when it is shared, and it does not get less.
4. Which line gives the idea that God is impartial?
‘Balanced and just are all of God’s decrees.’
5. What message does the poet give us through this poem?
Kindness, generosity and forgiveness create happiness; noble deeds inspire other noble deeds.
6. Which line do you like the most and why?
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: ‘As one lamp lights another, nor grows less, So nobleness enkindleth nobleness.’ I like it because it shows that goodness spreads when we share it.
7. Try to dramatize the poem. Use body language, facial expressions, and perform the poem.
Activity: students dramatize the poem in groups. Marks as per the teacher’s evaluation.
Complete the summary of the poem by filling in the blanks (p. 30–31)

On a pleasant and quiet night, a desperate ……… goes to the tent of ……… He begs ……… to protect him from the ……… who were after him. Yussouf readily grants what he wants. He ……… the guest that night. Before the sun rises, he wakes him up and gives him his swiftest ……… and some ………. The guest’s heart moves and makes him ……… that he had killed Yussouf’s son. But, to his surprise, Yussouf gives him thrice the gold and tells him to go away before the enemy ……… him.
stranger; Yussouf; shelter; enemies; entertains; horse; gold; confess; catches

lessons.t: Unit 7 · The Will of Sacrifice (Prose) & The Song of Freedom (Poem – Memorization)
lessons.au: Letters of Bhagat Singh (Prose); C. Subramanya Bharathi, tr. Prema Nandakumar (Poem)
lessons.words: British India – India under the British rule; well-known – famous, widely known; response – reply; revolutionary – involving violence; initiate – to make somebody a member of a particular group; terrorists – persons who use violence to achieve their aims; legitimate – lawful, regular; violence – behaviour that is intended to hurt or kill somebody; thinker – a person who thinks in a particular way; steep in – to be deeply involved; socialist – one who advocates socialism; common – (here) shared by all; pamphlets – leaflets; turbulent – violent situation; brutal – savage; veteran – one with long experience of service; enslaved – made into a slave; aggressive – attacking; shaheed – martyr; condemn – sentenced to punishment; noose – knot around the neck; anxious – troubled; fortunate – lucky; transportation – sending criminals to a place far away as a form of punishment; calamity – great misfortune; dingy – dark and dirty; comrades – mates or fellow associates; conceal – hide, keep secret; elevate – lift up, raise; will – death note; symbol – sign; collective – shared by all; blissful – extremely happy and peaceful; subservience – a state in which you do whatever someone else wants you to do; trickster’s sway – power or influence of one who deceives or cheats people; conch – the shell of a sea animal which produces a sound when you blow into it; deceit – behaviour that is deliberately intended to mislead people; glutton – one who eats too much in a greedy way; rake – one who behaves in an immoral way; weal – well-being; enslave – make into a slave; sole – exclusive, only
lessons.notes: Unit 7 has a prose piece on the life of Shaheed Bhagat Singh (pp. 32–43), with his two letters from prison: the first to his fellow revolutionary Batukeshwar Dutt, and the second to his comrades. Bhagat Singh believed that the value of a man lies in what he gives, not in what he receives. The poem 'The Song of Freedom' by C. Subramanya Bharathi (pp. 45–47, memorization) celebrates India’s independence, the end of foreign rule, caste pride and deceit, and the equality of all people. The lesson also covers homophones and phrasal verbs, and seeking information through dialogues.
ab: Before you read – Blessed (p. 32)
1. Why does the poet think that he is blessed?
The poet thinks he is blessed because he was born in this land and had the luck to love her.
2. What is very precious for the poet?
The living wealth of her love (the love for his motherland) is very precious for the poet.
3. Why does the poet value ‘living wealth’ more than ‘queenly treasure’? Discuss in groups.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: The living wealth of love brings lasting joy and the feeling of belonging. A queenly treasure can be lost or spent, but love for one’s land and people cannot be bought with money.
Check your comprehension – Share your responses (p. 34)
1. Who actively participated in the freedom struggle from Bhagat Singh’s family?
His grandfather Arjan Singh, his father Kishan Singh and his uncle Ajit Singh were all active in the freedom struggle.
2. Name the political leaders who were in contact with Bhagat Singh when he was in DAV School in Lahore.
Lala Lajpat Rai and Ras Bihari Bose.
3. How did Bhagat Singh respond to Gandhiji’s call?
He left his school in 1921 in response to Gandhiji’s call for non-cooperation and joined the National School at Lahore.
4. Where did Bhagat Singh come in contact with Bhagwati Charan and Sukhdev?
He came in contact with Bhagwati Charan and Sukhdev at the National School, Lahore, which was a centre of revolutionary activities.
5. Why is Bhagat Singh remembered even today?
He is remembered as a bold revolutionary figure and as a great thinker who was steeped in socialist thought.
6. Who did Bhagat Singh want to take revenge on? Why?

He wanted to take revenge on Deputy Inspector General Scott, because Scott was responsible for the death of Lala Lajpat Rai after a brutal police attack. By mistake, he shot Assistant Superintendent Saunders instead.
7. According to Bhagat Singh, where does the value of man lie?
According to Bhagat Singh, the value of a man lies not in what he is capable of receiving but in what he is capable of giving.
Letter – 1 · Share your responses (p. 35)
1. What was the only prayer of the people who were with Bhagat Singh?
Their only prayer was that somehow or other they must escape the noose (the gallows).
2. What do you mean by the phrase ‘transportation for life’?
It means being sent to a faraway place (a prison, such as the Andamans) to spend the rest of one’s life as a punishment.
3. What kind of punishment does Bhagat Singh talk about?
He talks about death by hanging (the death sentence) and transportation for life (life imprisonment).
4. What expectations did Bhagat Singh have from the people who escaped the gallows of death?
He expected them to live and show the world that revolutionaries can face every calamity, bear the worst tortures in prison and not escape worldly difficulties by death.
Letter – 2 · Check your comprehension – Share your responses (p. 37)
1. What kind of life did Bhagat Singh desire to lead?
He did not want to live as a prisoner or under restrictions. He wanted to live a free life so that he could fulfil his ambitions for humanity and his country.
2. Bhagat Singh’s name has become a symbol of… a. elevation b. relaxation c. revolution d. reorientation
c. revolution
3. Bhagat Singh was never afraid of meeting… a. friends b. death c. enemies d. relatives
b. death
4. Bhagat Singh is a model of… a. social service b. political wisdom c. oration d. sacrifice
d. sacrifice
5. ‘If I live I might perhaps get a chance to fulfil them’. a. What wishes did he want to fulfil? b. Who is he telling this?

a. He wanted to fulfil his ambitions to do something for humanity and his country.
b. He is telling this to his comrades (the fellow convicts).
6. Why did Bhagat Singh feel proud of himself?
He felt proud because he was ready to mount the gallows boldly and with a smile, which he believed would inspire others to sacrifice their lives for the freedom of the country.
Think about the text – C1 (p. 38)
1. How did Bhagat Singh participate in the freedom struggle?

He left his school to join the National School, came in contact with revolutionaries, became a member of the Hindustan Republican Association, took part in revolutionary activities, and wrote letters, pamphlets and articles on freedom and socialism.
2. What made the revolutionaries use guns and bombs against the British?
They believed that British rule was unjust and oppressive, so they felt it was legitimate to use violence to overthrow the foreigners.
3. What are the means of production, according to Bhagat Singh?
According to him, the means of production are land, labour and capital.
4. How was Bhagat Singh able to keep the spark of freedom struggle alive?
He kept the spark alive through his letters written from jail, in which he wrote about freedom and the longing for a change for the better.
5. Why is Bhagat Singh remembered even today?
He is remembered as a bold revolutionary, a great thinker steeped in socialist thought, and a martyr who sacrificed his life for the nation.
Think about the text – C2 (p. 39)
1. What were the incidents that brought changes in Bhagat Singh’s life?

The brutal police attack on Lala Lajpat Rai at an anti-British procession, which led to his death on November 17, 1928, and the incident in which Bhagat Singh threw bombs in the Central Assembly Hall.
2. How would you have tried Bhagat Singh if you were the judge in the British Court?

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: I would consider his actions as violence against the government, but also his motive of freedom for the nation. I would give a sentence keeping in mind the law and his intentions.
3. “The value of a man lies not in what he is capable of receiving, but in what he is capable of giving.” Discuss with your classmates.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: A person is valued for the service and sacrifice he gives to others, such as sharing knowledge, helping the needy and working for the nation, rather than for the wealth he receives.
4. Write a letter to your friend about your patriotic feeling, after reading the letters of Bhagat Singh.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: Dear friend, after reading the letters of Bhagat Singh, I feel proud of our freedom fighters. I want to serve my country by studying well, being honest and helping others. Yours, Ravi.
Vocabulary – V1. Match adjectives in column A with words in column B (p. 39)
1. revolutionary
e. ideas (revolutionary ideas)
2. collective
a. effort (collective effort)
3. turbulent
g. waters (turbulent waters)
4. conditional
f. reflexes (conditional reflexes)
5. freedom
c. struggle (freedom struggle)
6. dingy
b. room (dingy room)
7. wet
d. floor (wet floor)
Vocabulary – V2. Substitute the underlined words with phrasal verbs (p. 40)
1. A committee has been set up to examine the problem.
look into
2. They managed to extinguish the fire after ten hours.
put out
3. Lots of people arrived for the music concert.
turned up
4. True friends support one another in times of need.
stand by
5. Whatever the temptation, he won’t yield to corruption.
give in
Speak well – Seeking information: Task 1 (Dialogue 1, p. 40–41)
Read the conversation between Sneha and Prema. Take roles and practise.
Practice activity in pairs. No fixed answer. Model: Sneha – ‘How much do they charge to teach driving?’ Prema – ‘They charge Rs. 2000 for ten hours.’
Speak well – Seeking information: Task 1 (Dialogues 2 and 3, p. 41–42)
Read the dialogues about Hampi and the railway station. Take roles and practise by changing the roles.
Practice activity in pairs. No fixed answer. Model: Tourist – ‘Excuse me, how far is the railway station from here?’ Giridhar – ‘It is about three kilometres.’
Speak well – Activities (p. 42)
1. Imagine you are Rajesh, gone to the grocery shop to buy things for bisibele bath. Have a simple and interesting conversation with the shopkeeper.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: Rajesh – ‘Good morning. I need rice, dal, tamarind, and some vegetables for bisibele bath.’ Shopkeeper – ‘Here you are. Anything else?’ Rajesh – ‘Yes, please give me some curry leaves and a packet of masala powder.’
2. Have a conversation with your loving sister about the plants you have grown in your kitchen garden.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
3. Your parents are refusing to send you for your school trip. Write a dialogue on how you convince them.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: Child – ‘Papa, the school trip will help me learn many things. I will take care of myself and call you every day.’ Parent – ‘But it is far.’ Child – ‘Our teacher will be with us, and I promise to be careful.’
Practise writing – Group work (p. 43)
Write a dialogue based on any ONE of the above situations (with at least 5–6 exchanges). Present it in the class and enact it.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.

Self-assessment: tick ‘Yes’, ‘No’ or ‘To some extent’ for: I was able to write a dialogue with 5–6 exchanges; I included appropriate questions and responses; I used contracted forms; I can read the dialogue aloud with proper pronunciation, stress and intonation.
Self-check by the student. No fixed answer.
Poetry – Before you read: A. Look at the pictures (p. 44)
Look at the pictures below. What do they suggest? Share your responses in groups or pairs.

Picture A shows people under harsh control (a man with a whip over a group of people), which suggests the cruelty and oppression of foreign rule. Picture B shows people celebrating with song and dance and birds flying free, which suggests freedom and joy after independence.
images/class-9/english/c9-en-l07-oppression.webp
images/class-9/english/c9-en-l07-celebration.webp
Poetry – Before you read: B. Flowers of India (p. 44)
Read the poem ‘Flowers of India’. What is its theme? What message does it convey?
Theme: the rich culture, unity and peace of India, which spreads all over the world. Message: Indians should spread peace, harmony and their culture, and help people who are in pain.
Understand the poem – The Song of Freedom (p. 47)

1. Fill in the blanks with the words given in brackets: In this poem, the poet celebrates the ……… of our nation. It is celebrated with songs and ……… Indians fought for the freedom unitedly leaving ……… to anyone. We are free from the tricks any ……… could play to divide us. [No chance, freedom, trickster, dance]
freedom; dance; no chance; trickster
2. This poem celebrates India’s freedom from the British rule. a. Quote the lines that refer to freedom.
‘For blissful freedom Is ours at last’; ‘Freedom is our universal speech’; ‘No nation shall enslave us again’.
2. b. What, according to the poet, is freedom?
According to the poet, freedom is a universal speech (understood by all), and equality is the experienced grace. Freedom means the end of foreign might, caste pride, deceit and slavery.
2. c. How does he want to celebrate it?
He wants to celebrate it with song and dance, by blowing the conch of victory and publishing the truth to all.
3. What does the poet mean by ‘the universal speech’ and ‘experienced grace’?
‘Universal speech’ means freedom is a language that all people can understand and share. ‘Experienced grace’ means equality that people have actually lived and enjoyed.

4. This poem is not just a description of free India. It is also a description of a glorious India. Do you agree? If so, which are the undesirable elements that the poet desires to free ourselves from?

Yes. The undesirable elements are caste-born pride, the foreigner’s might, passive subservience, the trickster’s sway, lie and deceit, the glutton and the rake, and the idler who lives on the work of others.
5. What differences do you see between ‘the India’ visualized by the poet and the present one?

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: The poet visualized an India of equality, truth, honesty, honour for workers and no caste pride or deceit. Today some of these problems, such as caste discrimination, corruption and inequality, still exist, though India is free.
Read and appreciate – The Song of Freedom (p. 48)
1. Look at stanza two. Which words are repeated? What effect does this repetition have on the reader?

The word ‘Gone’ is repeated (‘Gone are those days…’, ‘Gone is the foreigner’s might’, ‘Gone is passive subservience’, ‘Gone is the trickster’s sway’). The repetition emphasizes that all the evils of the old days have ended and it creates a joyful rhythm for the reader.
2. a. What images can you visualize when you read: ‘This is the hour of song and dance.’
People singing and dancing together in celebration of freedom.
2. b. What images can you visualize when you read: ‘We’ll blow the conch of victory.’
People blowing a conch shell to announce victory and the success of the freedom struggle.
2. c. What images can you visualize when you read: ‘Now lie and deceit are dead.’
Falsehood and cheating disappearing, like a dead thing that no longer harms anyone.
2. d. What images can you visualize when you read: ‘Honour to the ploughman and the worker.’
A farmer ploughing his field and workers doing their labour, being respected by all.
Self-check – The Song of Freedom (memorization)
Memorize the poem ‘The Song of Freedom’ and recite it in the class.
Activity: the student recites the poem from memory. Marks as per the teacher’s evaluation.

iq.q: ಚಿತ್ರವನ್ನು ನೋಡಿ ಉತ್ತರಿಸಿ: Look at picture B. What are the people doing?
iq.a: They are celebrating by singing, dancing and raising their hands.

iq.q: ಚಿತ್ರವನ್ನು ನೋಡಿ ಉತ್ತರಿಸಿ: Look at picture A. What is the man in the hat holding in his hand?
iq.a: A whip (a stick or whip raised over the people).

lessons.t: Unit 8 · To My Countrymen (Prose) & It Never Comes Again (Poem – Memorization)
lessons.au: Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam (Prose); Richard Henry Stoddard (Poem)
lessons.words: affordable – having enough money to buy or pay for something; habitat – a place to live; perpetuate – continue to exist for a long time; mission – an important assignment; dwell upon – think or talk about something; disposed to – want to do something, inclined; nurture – help a plan or idea to develop; revive – make something strong again; demonstrate – show; remote – far away, not likely; core – the most important; multifaceted – having many parts or sides; cut across – if a problem or feeling cuts across different groups of people, they are all affected by it; access – use something; dot – if an area is dotted with things, there are a lot of them there; untapped – not yet used; potential – to have a natural ability or quality; channel (v) – direct something such as money or energy towards a particular purpose; insurgency – rebellion, an attempt by a group of people to take control of their government using force and violence; unrest – protest or violent behaviour; intellectual – an intelligent, well-educated person; ingredient – a quality you need to achieve something; hypothesis – an idea that is not yet proved (plural: hypotheses); enterprise – a project that is difficult or requires effort; ignite – activate, burn; the heart of – the most important part of; substance of – the main part of; household name – a name that has become very well known; balms – something that helps you to relax; sterner – stronger; reign – period of rule; vanished – disappeared; sigh – a long deep breath showing disappointment; in vain – without success; behold – look at or see
lessons.notes: Unit 8 has an extract 'To My Countrymen' from Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam’s book 'Ignited Minds' (pp. 50–56). Dr Kalam dreams of a literate, poverty-free and developed India, and says that missions are bigger than organizations and that the spirit of ‘India can do it’ must be revived. Students are asked to ignite their minds and think big. The poem 'It Never Comes Again' by Richard Henry Stoddard (pp. 67–68, memorization) says that youth is precious and, though many gains make up for losses, the loss of youth can never be made up. The lesson also covers phrasal verbs, idioms, collocations, conjunctions and modals.
ab: Before you read – Complete the passage (p. 50)

Complete the passage: I was born into a middle-class ……… family in the island town of Rameswaram in the erstwhile ……… state. My ……… Jainulabdeen, had neither much formal education nor much ……… He had an ideal helpmate in my ……… Ashiamma. I do not recall the exact number of people she ……… every day, but I am quite certain that far more ……… were with us than all the ……… of our own family put together.
Tamil; Madras; father; wealth; mother; fed; outsiders; members
Check your Understanding (p. 56)
1. What, according to Dr Kalam, is important in life to become a winner?
The power of imagination, which lies at the heart of the creative process, is what makes the difference between winners and losers.
2. Which is bigger, the individual or the organization?
The organization is bigger than the individual who runs it. The mission is bigger than the organization.
3. What can be achieved by working together?
Big missions can be achieved, such as generating 200,000 MW of power, a second green revolution, affordable medical facilities and taking man to Mars.
4. It helped us humble a mighty empire. Who does the phrase ‘mighty empire’ refer to?
The phrase refers to the British Empire (British rule in India).
5. What will happen if we have a low aim?
The possibility of India becoming a leading nation (building cars, satellites and power stations for other nations) will remain remote.
6. What is Dr Kalam’s view on the good progress we have made in the software sector?
Dr Kalam says that we have made good progress in software, but almost all the hardware is imported. We must rise higher on the value scale.
7. Mention the states that are faring better than others in the country.
Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab and Karnataka (and the business hubs Bengaluru, Chennai, Mumbai, Delhi and Hyderabad).
8. Which state is rich in mineral wealth and natural gas?
Tripura.
9. Where do you see insurgency and unrest among people?
In Assam.

10. Match the following: 1. Acharya P. C. Ray 2. J.N. Tata 3. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan 4. Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya | a. Banaras Hindu University b. Aligarh Muslim University c. Chemical and pharmaceutical industries d. Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru
1 – c (Chemical and pharmaceutical industries); 2 – d (Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru); 3 – b (Aligarh Muslim University); 4 – a (Banaras Hindu University).
Think about the text (p. 57)
1. What do people expect from biotechnology labs and medical councils?

People expect biotechnology labs and medical councils to serve their real purpose: to set up advanced medical facilities, proper diagnostic facilities and affordable drugs for the masses at reasonable prices.
2. What is Dr Abdul Kalam’s vision of India in 2020?
He wishes to see a literate and poverty-free India governed by noble leaders, and a system where scientists and technologists work on missions relevant to the common man.
3. How did great people such as J.N. Tata, Sir Syed Ahmad Khan, etc. help India come up in the world?

J.N. Tata brought the steel industry to India and founded the Indian Institute of Science. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan set up Aligarh Muslim University. Acharya P.C. Ray nurtured the chemical and pharmaceutical industries, and Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya founded Banaras Hindu University. They were motivated by the spirit of ‘India can do it’.
4. As mentioned in the lesson, what is it that we have? What is it that we don’t have?
We have multifaceted manpower, basic infrastructure and core competence. We don’t have an integrated action plan, a shared national vision and the drive to set high aims (the spirit of enterprise).
5. What is his message to teachers and students?
Students should get ready to transform India into a developed nation. They should ignite their minds and think big. Teachers should be such gurus who can shape the character of a child.
6. What is lacking in the discussions and debates that take place in intellectual forums, political platforms and academic institutions?
Though there are endless debates and arguments, there is little progress. The theme of a developed India is not discussed seriously, and people do not take responsibility or act on it.
Speak well – Speech (p. 57)
Find a partner and speak on the topic ‘The country of my dreams’ for three minutes. Change the partner and speak for two minutes, then for one minute.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: My country of dreams is a clean, literate and poverty-free nation where every child gets good education, every citizen has equal opportunity and the nation is known for its science, honesty and love for one another.
Speak well – Interview (p. 57–58)
Write down three to four questions you would have liked to ask Dr Kalam if he had visited your school. Conduct an interview with one person playing the role of Dr Kalam.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model questions: 1. What inspired you to become a scientist? 2. How can students become good citizens? 3. What is your advice for students who want to achieve big goals?
Take the roles of the Interviewer and Dr Kalam and practise asking and answering questions (interview from DNA newspaper).
Practice activity in pairs. Model: Interviewer – ‘What are your favourite leisure-time activities?’ Kalam – ‘Books are my favourite friends.’
Study the words – Phrasal verbs: Refer to a dictionary and make sentences (p. 59)
Make sentences using the phrasal verbs: set aside, set about, set forth, set out, set down, set in, set off.

1. We set aside some money every month for books. 2. They set about cleaning the classroom after lunch. 3. He set forth his plan clearly in the meeting. 4. We set out for the temple early in the morning. 5. Please set down your ideas in writing. 6. The rainy season has set in. 7. The crackers were set off on Diwali night.
Study the words – Collocations: A. Match the words that collocate (p. 60)
Match the words: noble, make, manufacture, launch, generate, face, take, developed, responsibility, satellites, challenges, power, cars, nation, leaders, efforts.
make – efforts; manufacture – cars; launch – satellites; generate – power; face – challenges; take – responsibility; developed – nation; noble – leaders.
Study the words – Collocations: B. Which prepositions go with which words? (p. 61)
Box A: dream, convert, consist, basis, willing, speak, give birth, worthy, have access. Box B: about, of, for, into, to.
dream of; convert into; consist of; basis for; willing to; speak about; give birth to; worthy of; have access to.
Study the words – Conjunctions (p. 61)
Why is the word ‘and’ used in the sentence ‘Missions need effort and the mind provides the purpose’?
‘And’ is a conjunction. It joins two parts of the sentence (two independent clauses) and adds extra information.
Can you make a list of all the conjunctions used in the lesson?
and, but, or, so, because, while, if, when, although, since, as, until, whereas, however, besides, so that, as soon as, unless, where, whenever.
Quiz – Conjunctions: Replace the wrong conjunctions with the most appropriate ones (p. 63)
1. I will go to bed now, or my homework is not done. (if, and, but)
but
2. Would you like to have tea and coffee? (but, or, and)
or
3. My sister wants both a bicycle although a book for her birthday. (and, in addition to, besides)
and
4. Ramya is very tall so that Parveen is very short. (if, until, while)
while
5. I came early until I can talk to you personally. (so that, as if, in spite of)
so that
6. Whoever she calls me, I feel happy. (whichever, whenever, wherever)
whenever
7. Although the class starts, you will not be able to play. (once, whereas, while)
once
8. Since I had seen that movie three times, I watched it again. (because, until, although)
although
Language in use – Modals (p. 63)
The word ‘must’ indicates necessity and is called a modal. Can you list the modals used in the lesson?
should, have to, need to, must, may, can, could, might (and needn’t, can’t, shouldn’t).
Quiz – Modals: Choose the appropriate modals to complete the sentences (p. 64)
1. _____ you speak Chinese? No, _____.
Can; I can’t.
2. I _____ study well for the exam.
must
3. _____ I borrow your pen?
May
4. We _____ watch TV so much.
shouldn’t
5. We _____ buy that bag. It’s expensive.
can’t
6. You _____ come to school in time.
must
7. I _____ work hard to complete the project.
have to
8. You _____ speak politely to others.
should
Let us write – Biography of Dr Abdul Kalam (p. 65–66)
Write a short biography/profile of Dr Abdul Kalam in your group, add the given points and prepare a fair copy. Also collect more information and present the biography to the class.

ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam (born 15 October 1931) was one of India’s most distinguished scientists, known as the ‘Missile Man of India’. He developed India’s first satellite launch vehicle, SLV-3, served as the eleventh President of India and received the Bharat Ratna in 1997. He wrote books such as ‘Wings of Fire’ and ‘India 2020’.
Project work: Collect the biographies of famous personalities and present them in the class.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
Before you read – The poem ‘It Never Comes Again’ (p. 67)
1. Whose loss, do you think, is the greatest?
Mohan’s loss, of his mother, is the greatest, because it cannot be replaced.
2. Why do you think the loss of other things is not that important?
Other things, like a cricket bat, a story book or stamps, can be bought or replaced, so their loss is not as important as losing a loved one.
3. Which of the losses can be compensated and which cannot be?
The loss of the cricket bat, the story book and the stamps can be compensated by buying new ones. The loss of a mother cannot be compensated.
Understand the poem (p. 68)
1. What happens when youth departs?
When youth departs, it takes something from our hearts, and it never comes again.
2. How does a person feel when he is youthful?
A youthful person feels full of dreams and strength, and life feels sweet and full of hope.
3. The poet says, ‘We sigh in vain.’ Why?
Because youth, once gone, can never come back, so the sighs bring no result.
4. Where does a person look for youth, after it is gone?
The person looks for it everywhere, on the earth and in the air, but it never comes again.
5. Why does the poet compare losses and gains with youth?
Gains can make up for many losses, but nothing can make up for the loss of youth, which is precious.
6. What is the message of the poem?
Youth is precious and cannot be regained. We should make the best use of our youth.
Read and appreciate (p. 69)
A. 1. The poet describes youth as ‘something sweet’. Do you agree with him? Why? Discuss in groups.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: Yes. Youth is a sweet time full of dreams and energy, so the poet is right to call it sweet.
A. 2. The poet says, ‘There are gains for all our losses.’ Do you agree? Give reasons.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: Partly. Many losses can be compensated by gains, but the loss of youth cannot be compensated.
A. 3. Which line/s do you like the most? Why?
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು.
A. 4. Can you think of some proverbs or quotations related to the theme of the poem?
Time and tide wait for none. (Other examples: Make hay while the sun shines; Youth is the time to study and to serve.)
Figures of speech – Metaphor and Personification (p. 69–70)
Example: ‘But when youth, the dream, departs…’
Metaphor. Youth is compared indirectly with a dream (the comparison is implied).
Example: ‘It takes something from our hearts.’
Personification. Youth, an abstract notion, is given the quality of a living being that takes something from our hearts.
Pick out other examples of personification from the poem.
‘Followed youth, with flying feet’ – youth is given feet, like a living being that runs away.
Collect some examples for metaphor and personification.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: Metaphor – ‘Tippu Sultan was the tiger of Mysuru.’ Personification – ‘The wind whispered through the trees.’
Rhyming words (p. 70)
Make a list of rhyming words from the poem (e.g. pain – reign). Add a few rhyming words to: sweet, air, heart, vanish.

From the poem: pain – again – reign – vain; sweet – feet; heart – part; air – everywhere. Added: sweet – meet, treat, sheet; air – care, fair, hair, there; heart – art, start, apart; vanish – banish, Spanish.

lessons.t: Supplementary Reading · Ranji’s Wonderful Bat (Ruskin Bond) & Monday Morning (Mark Twain)
lessons.au: Ruskin Bond (Ranji’s Wonderful Bat); Mark Twain (Monday Morning)
lessons.words: confidence – the quality of being certain of your abilities; innings – the period in a game of cricket in which a team or a player bats; awning – a sheet of canvas on a frame, used for shelter; gloves – a piece of leather/cloth keepers wear in cricket; growl – to make a low rough sound, usually in anger; glare – a long angry look; century – a score of hundred runs by one player in cricket; lend – to give something to someone for a short period of time; delight – happiness; twist – to give a sudden quick turn; streak – to move somewhere extremely quickly; stumps – the three vertical wooden poles at which the ball is bowled in cricket; presently – very soon; ailment – illness; investigate – examine thoroughly; detect – discover; slight – very little; feeble – weak; groan/moan – give out a low cry of pain; occur – happen; in reserve – for future use; sore – painful; promising – bright, likely to succeed; symptom – sign; worthwhile – profitable; spirit – strength; stare – look with concentration; anxiously – worriedly, with concern; mortify – (here) die; restore – to become strong again; fright – great fear; ache – pain; row – noisy argument; miserable – very unhappy
lessons.notes: The supplementary readings are 'Ranji’s Wonderful Bat' by Ruskin Bond (pp. 72–77) and 'Monday Morning' by Mark Twain (pp. 78–82). Ranji, a young cricketer, loses confidence after a few poor scores. His friend Mr Kumar lends him a lucky old bat, and Ranji regains his confidence, which he realises was what he needed. In 'Monday Morning', Tom Sawyer pretends to be ill to avoid school, but his plan fails. The stories teach confidence, honesty and the value of hard work.
ab: Ranji’s Wonderful Bat – I. Answer in one or two sentences (p. 76)
1. Who was the youngest member of the team?
Ranji was the youngest member of the team. He was only eleven.
2. What did Mr Kumar give Ranji?
Mr Kumar gave Ranji one of his old cricket bats, the lucky one he had made a century with, and lent it to him for the rest of the cricket season.
3. How many runs did Ranji score in the first match?
In the first match with the lucky bat, Ranji scored 58 runs, not out.
4. Who was the captain of Ranji’s team?
Suraj was the captain of Ranji’s school team.
5. Why did Ranji buy two laddoos?
He bought two laddoos for Koki, the girl next door, as a thank-you for helping him practise and to share his happiness at the win.
6. Why was everyone pleased with Ranji after the second match?
Ranji scored forty in the next game and then forty-five in a two-day match. His coach, his captain and Mr Kumar were pleased with his good batting.
7. How did Ranji lose the bat?
He left the bat in the bus when he came home from the maidan.
8. What did Ranji do after the last match of the season?
He scored 75 runs with a bat borrowed from Suraj. Then he bought a dozen laddoos, six for Koki and six for Mr Kumar.
Ranji’s Wonderful Bat – II. Answer in three or four sentences (p. 77)
1. Why was Ranji upset after the game?

Ranji was upset because he had got out for no runs, he had not scored well in his last three matches, and he feared that he would be dropped from the team. He had been trying hard and practising regularly.
2. How did Mr Kumar help Ranji?
Mr Kumar lent Ranji his lucky old bat, the bat with which he had made a century, and told him that it would help him score runs. Later, he told Ranji that what he needed was confidence, not a bat.
3. Ranji scored many runs with the new bat given by Mr Kumar. What may be the reason?
Ranji believed that the bat was lucky, so he regained his confidence. Confidence made him play his strokes freely, and so he scored more runs.
4. How did Mr Kumar console Ranji when he lost the bat?
Mr Kumar said that any bat will do, a bat has magic only when the batsman has magic, what Ranji needed was confidence, and he had always been a good player.
5. What is the good quality you appreciate in Mr Kumar?
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: Mr Kumar is kind, encouraging and wise. He understands the feelings of a young player and helps him believe in himself.
6. If you were Mr Kumar, how would you help the boy?
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model: I would encourage him, tell him that he is a good player, help him practise regularly and build his confidence instead of depending on a lucky object.
7. What do we learn from the story?
We learn that confidence and hard work matter more than lucky objects. We should believe in ourselves and not give up after a failure.
Ranji’s Wonderful Bat – Activity (p. 77)

Collect the pictures of cricket players and make a scrap book with captions. Learn the actions which an umpire shows in a cricket match and make a list of them with the help of your physical education teacher.
ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಆಧರಿಸಿ ಅಂಕ ನೀಡುವುದು. Model umpire signals: ‘Out’ (raise a finger); ‘Six’ (both arms raised above the head); ‘Four’ (arm waved sideways); ‘Wide’ (both arms stretched out sideways).
Monday Morning – C1. Answer the following in one sentence each (p. 82)
1. How did Tom feel on Monday morning?
Tom felt miserable because Monday meant another week of school.
2. Why did he want to be sick?
He wanted to be sick so that he could stay home from school.
3. What made Tom think of his toe?
He remembered a doctor’s story about an ailment that kept a patient in bed for weeks and could make him lose a finger, so he thought his sore toe could be a useful ailment.
4. Why did he start groaning?
He groaned to make people believe that he was seriously ill and suffering.
5. What did he want Sid to do?
He wanted Sid to tell Aunt Polly about his ailment.
6. Was there anything really wrong with his toe?
No, there was nothing really wrong with his toe.
7. Did Aunt Polly believe that Tom was really dying?
No. She said, ‘Rubbish! I don’t believe it!’, but she still went upstairs anxiously.
8. What did Aunt Polly do when Tom said his toe was mortified?
She sank into a chair and laughed and cried together, and then she told Tom to stop his nonsense.
9. What did he complain of next?
He complained that one of his upper front teeth was loose and it ached terribly.
10. Did Tom’s plans finally succeed?
No. Aunt Polly tied the loose tooth with silk thread to the bedpost and pulled it out with burning coals, and Tom had to go to school.
Monday Morning – C2. Answer in two or three sentences each (p. 82)
1. What did Tom begin to investigate? Why?
Tom investigated every part of his body to find an ailment, so that he could stay at home from school.
2. Why did Tom try not to complain about his loose tooth?
Tom did not complain about his loose tooth because he feared that his aunt would pull it out, and that would hurt.
3. What happened when Tom thought that he had a stomach pain?
The stomach pain grew feeble and soon died away, so Tom gave up that ailment and searched for another one.
4. How did Aunt Polly pull out Tom’s tooth?

She tied one end of a silk thread to the loose tooth with a loop and the other end to the bedpost. Then she thrust a pan of burning coals close to his face, and the tooth came out dangling from the bedpost.
